articles.titulo: Reshaping the immunometabolic microenvironment via an inflammation-responsive magnesium delivery system to tackle bone diseases.
articles.autores: Li X, Shao H, … Qin L (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Recent advancements in magnesium (Mg)-based biomaterials have illuminated their role in immunomodulation. However, their effects on bone repair amid excessive inflammation have not been systematically explored. In this study, we demonstrate that magnesium ions (Mg2+) enhance bone turnover and counteract inflammatory bone loss in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced model. Mechanistically, Mg2+ improves mitochondrial metabolic efficiency in bone-forming cells, thereby mitigating oxidative stress caused by excessive inflammation and promoting cell survival. Consequently, the suppression of osteogenic differentiation is effectively reversed under excessive inflammatory conditions. Moreover, Mg2+ modulates the inflammatory microenvironment by enhancing the mitochondrial metabolism of macrophages under oxidative stress. This process facilitates M2 macrophage polarization and stimulates the production of reparative cytokines, such as BMP2, which in turn supports osteogenesis. Furthermore, Mg2+ significantly reduces mitochondrial respiration in osteoclasts and inhibits osteoclastogenesis. We further developed a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive Mg2+ delivery system that specifically targets inflammation-damaged cells and significantly enhances fracture healing under inflammatory conditions. Collectively, our findings highlight the potential of Mg-based biomaterials in the treatment of inflammatory bone diseases.

articles.titulo: Ecological drivers and spatiotemporal dynamics of Opisthorchis viverrini transmission in Southern Laos.
articles.autores: Revolteado MJ, Valencia J, … Sato M (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Opisthorchis viverrini remains a persistent public health problem in the Lower Mekong region, where transmission continues despite long-standing control efforts. Effective surveillance requires approaches capable of detecting environmental contamination and capturing temporal and ecological variation in transmission. We assessed the utility of environmental DNA (eDNA) for detecting O. viverrini and examined its ecological and spatiotemporal associations across freshwater systems in Champasak Province, southern Lao PDR. Water samples were collected from four endemic villages at four timepoints between May 2024 and February 2025. O. viverrini eDNA detection was assessed in relation to water physicochemical parameters, water source, village, and the presence of Bithynia spp., the first intermediate snail host. Generalized estimating equations (GEE), with site as the clustering variable, were used to assess associations while accounting for repeated observations within sites. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis provided an exploratory estimate of apparent model discrimination. Bithynia spp. presence was significantly associated with O. viverrini eDNA detection (OR = 3.15, 95% CI: 1.08-9.14; p = 0.035). Sampling timepoint was also associated with detection (p < 0.001). Compared with February 2025, the adjusted odds of detection were lower in May 2024 (OR = 0.013, 95% CI: 0.003-0.070) and August 2024 (OR = 0.061, 95% CI: 0.013-0.278), while the October 2024 contrast was not statistically significant (OR = 0.283, 95% CI: 0.074-1.080; p = 0.065). The fitted model had an apparent AUC of 0.833 (95% CI: 0.778-0.888), an exploratory estimate of discrimination in the analyzed dataset. O. viverrini eDNA detection was associated with Bithynia spp. presence and varied across sampling timepoints, indicating temporal and ecological heterogeneity in environmental occurrence. These temporal associations should be interpreted cautiously because site availability varied between sampling periods and spatial autocorrelation between sites was not explicitly modeled. Environmental eDNA may complement conventional surveillance by helping prioritize sites for further ecological and epidemiological investigation, but detection alone does not establish active local transmission or quantify transmission intensity.

articles.titulo: Vector-Borne Disease Education and Outreach in Arizona: A Qualitative Study of Stakeholder Perspectives.
articles.revista: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene
articles.autores: Finucane S, Robinson J, … Yeo S (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Successful public health messaging and education can reduce transmission of vector-borne diseases through improved identification and reporting of vectors, reduction in vector habitats, and increased use of personal protective measures. However, it is unclear how Arizona public health and vector control professionals perceive the effectiveness of their current dissemination strategies. We conducted 18 key informant interviews with health department and vector control professionals across Arizona to evaluate current dissemination messaging, materials, and channels and to identify key gaps and challenges. Results indicated that messaging primarily focused on mosquito-borne disease prevention, emphasizing source reduction and personal protective behaviors, and the Fight the Bite campaign was frequently cited. Education on disease symptoms, care-seeking behaviors, and tick-specific risks and prevention practices was less commonly reported. Handouts and flyers were the most common materials, primarily available in English and Spanish. One-on-one interactions and social media were viewed as the most successful dissemination channels. Outreach typically occurred during the monsoon season and in response to positive human cases and vectors. Major challenges included limited funding, staffing constraints, and low public risk perception. Future dissemination should prioritize creating engaging, locally relevant content and adapting strategies to effectively reach the local community. County health departments should also expand education on locally relevant tick-borne diseases, such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever. These findings highlight barriers and opportunities to strengthen public health messaging and dissemination for vector-borne diseases within Arizona.

articles.titulo: Rethinking type 2 diabetes: a bone marrow disease under metabolic disguise?
articles.autores: Fantuzzi F, Spigoni V, … Dei Cas A (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is traditionally viewed as a metabolic disorder driven by insulin resistance and progressive pancreatic β-cell failure. This review examines how metabolic stress remodels the bone marrow (BM) niche and whether these alterations contribute to inflammatory haematopoiesis, defective vascular repair and disease progression. The BM niche is a specialized microenvironment integrating endothelial, mesenchymal, neural, adipocytic, and immune components that cooperatively regulate hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) maintenance, mobilization and immune homeostasis. Evidence from animal models, together with more limited human observations, indicates that obesity-associated inflammation, lipotoxicity and hyperglycaemia can alter these compartments, favour myeloid-biased haematopoiesis and induce persistent metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. The resulting inflammatory myeloid output may subsequently amplify adipose-tissue and pancreatic islet inflammation, while vascular and autonomic niche dysfunction may constrain endogenous repair, creating bidirectional feedback between systemic metabolic dysfunction and the BM. We integrate these processes within diabet(ogen)ic nicheopathy, a proposed research framework encompassing BM alterations that may arise from and potentially reinforce metabolic disease. Particular attention is given to BM adipose tissue, BM-pancreas inflammatory crosstalk, progenitor mobilopathy and the therapeutic implications of BM programming. However, whether BM alterations precede overt T2D, contribute independently to its progression or predominantly reflect cumulative metabolic injury remains unresolved. The BM niche should therefore be regarded as an emerging mechanistic and therapeutic target rather than an established determinant of T2D progression.

articles.titulo: Live Imaging of Axon Growth in the Developing Drosophila Wing.
articles.autores: Saha S, Forghani R, Giniger E (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original: This protocol describes reproducible, high-resolution imaging of the growth of a single, identified pioneer axon in a developing animal. It uses the well-characterized TSM1 axon of the Drosophila wing to track morphological and cytoskeletal dynamics, as well as signaling processes for which fluorescent markers are available. Between 9 h and 12 h after puparium formation (APF), TSM1 grows nearly 120 µm and undergoes pathfinding to fasciculate with the central L3 nerve of the wing, distal to the guidepost GSR neuron. Imaging of TSM1 in wild-type tissue and following genetic or pharmacological perturbation has revealed morphological parameters of growth cone dynamics and demonstrated how signaling molecules, including the tyrosine kinase Abelson (Abl) and the actin polymerase Enabled (Ena), regulate actin organization within the growth cone. These molecules influence axon growth by redistributing actin mass, supporting filopodial protrusion, and promoting axon extension. In addition to cytoskeleton-dependent growth, recent studies have examined the effects of non-cytoskeletal factors, including NAD+ and Ca2+/calmodulin, on axon growth and branching. Although the precise mechanisms underlying axon growth and guidance remain incompletely understood, this in vivo imaging approach, combined with super-resolution microscopy, provides a platform for identifying additional pathways that regulate them.

articles.titulo: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Behrens C, Chatterjee M, … Sheehan MJ (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

articles.titulo: Non-falciparum malaria and the blind spot of HRP2 based rapid diagnostic tests: a nationally representative PCR study of children in the 2024-25 Uganda Malaria Indicator Survey.
articles.autores: Nantalaga KC, Nantege A, Nabirye M (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria diagnosis in Uganda rests almost entirely on rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detecting histidine rich protein 2 (HRP2), an antigen expressed only by Plasmodium falciparum. Infections with non-falciparum species are therefore invisible to the national testing algorithm by design. Using a subsample of 466 children from the 2013-14 Democratic Republic of the Congo Demographic and Health Survey, Doctor and colleagues concluded that the risk of missing infections through falciparum-specific RDT use was low, but that conclusion rested on only eight non-falciparum mono-infections. No nationally representative estimate exists for Uganda.
We analysed the 2024-25 Uganda Malaria Indicator Survey, in which children aged 6 to 59 months were tested by HRP2 based RDT and by real time PCR with species determination. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence of each species, alone and in mixed infection, and calculated RDT sensitivity separately for P. falciparum mono-infections, mixed infections containing P. falciparum, and non-falciparum mono-infections.
Among 6975 children, weighted parasite prevalence by PCR was 17.5% (95% confidence interval (CI) 15.6 to 19.4). Non-falciparum species were involved in 2.72% (95% CI 2.25 to 3.19) of children and were the sole species in 1.03% (95% CI 0.75 to 1.30). Weighted prevalence of mono-infection was 0.69% (95% CI 0.47 to 0.90) for P. malariae, 0.30% (95% CI 0.14 to 0.46) for P. ovale, and 4 of 6,975 children (exact 95% CI 0.016 to 0.147%) for P. vivax. RDT sensitivity was 82.3% (95% CI 80.0 to 84.6) for P. falciparum mono-infections and 90.7% (95% CI 84.6 to 95.0) for mixed infections containing P. falciparum, but only 14.3% (95% CI 7.1 to 24.7) for non-falciparum mono-infections. Of 267 PCR confirmed infections missed by the RDT, 60 (22.5%) were non-falciparum mono-infections.
Approximately one Ugandan child in a hundred carries a malaria infection that HRP2 based RDTs cannot detect, and such infections account for more than a fifth of all infections the RDT misses. Our estimates confirm, with nearly nine times as many events, the direction of previous findings from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, but they place the absolute burden in a national context that the earlier subsample could not support. This is a structural limitation of the diagnostic, not a failure of test quality, and it will not be resolved by improving HRP2 test performance.

articles.titulo: Development, Characterization and Evaluation of a Stable Eucalyptus globulus Essential Oil-Permethrin Nanoemulsion with Repellent Activity Against Aedes aegypti.
articles.autores: Firoozfar F, Fatemi M, … Moosa-Kazemi SH (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Aedes aegypti is a primary vector of several clinically significant arboviruses. This study aimed to develop a nanoemulsion-based co-delivery system incorporating permethrin and Eucalyptus globulus essential oil for mosquito repellent applications.
The essential oil composition of E. globulus was determined using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Nanoemulsions were formulated using a low-energy spontaneous emulsification method and characterized for stability, droplet size distribution and zeta potential. The optimal formulation was further examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and evaluated for cytotoxicity. The repellent activity of eucalyptus essential oil, permethrin, their combinations, and the eucalyptus essential oil-permethrin nanoemulsion was assessed against female Ae. aegypti mosquitoes using the arm-in-cage assay.
The nanoemulsions exhibited a mean droplet size of 93.5 nm and a zeta potential of 60-70 mV, indicating good stability. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed the presence of spherical and uniformly dispersed droplets. The eucalyptus essential oil-permethrin nanoemulsion demonstrated strong repellency. A 3% permethrin concentration in the eucalyptus-permethrin nanoemulsion provided the maximum protection rate at 91.8%. In stability testing, the 1.5% version of the same nanoemulsion proved to be the most stable.
Eucalyptus globulus essential oil, especially in nanoemulsion form and combined with permethrin, shows promise as a natural repellent formulation against Ae. aegypti. However, field trials are essential to confirm these findings under natural conditions.

articles.titulo: Gut permeability and endotoxemia in obesity.
articles.autores: Fajkić A, Belančić A, … Lam YW (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Obesity is increasingly recognized as an immunometabolic disorder in which chronic low-grade inflammation is sustained by persistent upstream triggers rather than by adiposity alone. A central candidate trigger is intestinal barrier dysfunction with metabolic endotoxemia, defined as chronic, subclinical elevations of gut-derived microbial components, most notably lipopolysaccharide (LPS), in the absence of overt infection. In obesity, the intestinal barrier shifts toward increased functional permeability through coordinated remodeling of tight junction organization, mucus layer destabilization, and epithelial stress responses. This creates permissive conditions for microbial ligand passage while mucosal architecture can remain grossly intact. Importantly, systemic exposure is not determined solely by permeability, but by a coupled system involving luminal LPS availability, lipid-facilitated epithelial uptake and export, and context-dependent partitioning and clearance of LPS through binding proteins, lipoproteins, and hepatic handling. Low-dose, repeated LPS signaling engages innate immune pathways (including TLR4 and inflammasome-associated programs), amplifying cytokine production and stress kinase activity that impairs insulin signaling across metabolic tissues. The resulting organ crosstalk within the gut-liver-adipose axis helps explain heterogeneity in metabolic trajectories among individuals with comparable body mass index, particularly when visceral adiposity and postprandial lipid flux are considered. Therapeutic strategies that converge on this axis, including dietary fiber enrichment, microbiota-targeted interventions, metabolic pharmacotherapy, and bariatric procedures, provide proof of reversibility, yet human evidence remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and incomplete causal inference. Advancing the field will require standardized, dynamic barrier phenotyping, longitudinal designs, and stratified intervention trials to identify gut-driven subgroups and enable precision approaches to obesity-related cardiometabolic disease.

articles.titulo: The gut microbiota of Brandt's vole under varying population densities reveals contrasting patterns in the natural environment.
articles.autores: Hilal MG, Tang K, … Wang D (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
The population density of rodents fluctuates due to intrinsic and extrinsic factors, inducing density-dependent effects on organisms and their habitats. The gut microbiota of herbivores plays a pivotal role in digestion, immunity, environmental adaptation, and host fitness. Crowding and host population density are considered among the driving factors that influence the gut microbiome of rodents. In laboratory settings, the gut microbiome of Brandt's voles exhibits distinct responses to density and crowding, which is a controlled environment and cannot mimic the natural system; however, its response in natural settings remains underexplored, which is more complex and shaped by biotic and abiotic interactions. Our study provides a comprehensive profiling of the (Lasiopodomys brandtii) gut microbiome at various population densities, under natural conditions, where diet and social structure fluctuate dynamically.
Across all densities, the dominant bacterial phyla were Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, Desulfobacterota, Campylobacterota, Actinobacteriota, and Patescibacteria. The Patescibacteria were significantly lower at medium (0.57% ± 0.117) and high densities (0.65% ± 0.423) than at low density (0.93% ± 0.339), whereas the Proteobacteria were higher at medium density (0.84% ± 0.518) than at low (0.43% ± 0.18) and high (0.54% ± 0.34) densities. Clostridia_vadinBB60 and F082 were reduced at high density relative to low and medium densities, and Lactobacillus abundance was lower at medium density compared with low and high densities. The microbial biomarkers at each density were (p < 0.05, LDA > 3): (Low; Bacilli, Helicobacter, Clostridiales_vadinBB60, F082, and Saccharimonadia), (Medium; Christensenellaceae), (High; Lactobacillus, Prevotella, and Lachnospiraceae). Alpha diversity was significantly lower at high density than at low and medium densities. At high density, Pielou's evenness, Shannon diversity index, observed richness, and Simpson's diversity were significantly lower than at low and medium densities (p < 0.05). Community structure differed significantly between low and high densities and between medium and high densities, but was similar between low and medium densities (p < 0.05). Bacterial predicted functional pathways varied significantly between low and medium densities and between high and medium densities, but showed no differences between low and high densities (p < 0.05). Density, AP, and pH were primary drivers of variance in microbial communities (p < 0.05). Mantel tests show that gut microbial diversity of voles is significantly correlated with density (r = 0.26, p = 0.0006) and water content (r = 0.19, p = 0.025), and microbial abundance is associated with soil water content (r = 0.26, p = 0.001) and aboveground biomass (AGB) (r = 0.24, p = 0.001). Density negatively affects microbial communities while positively affecting the soil physicochemical factors.
This study demonstrates that host population density serves as the primary driver of variation in gut microbiome in wild Brandt's voles. Soil properties and plant biomass act as secondary environmental filters. This work underscores the central role of host population dynamics in shaping the gut microbiome in natural systems, with potential implications for understanding how crowding stress influences host-microbe interactions in wild small mammals.

articles.titulo: Sanghuang polysaccharides as emerging immunomodulators: linking molecular structure, immune recognition and the gut microbiota-immune axis.
articles.autores: Ma X, Chen X, … Gong N (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Sanghuang - a group of medicinal polypores now taxonomically reassigned from Phellinus linteus sensu lato to the genus Sanghuangporus - has been used for two millennia in East Asian medicine, and its polysaccharides are now recognized as the principal immunologically active constituents. Yet the field remains fragmented: "Sanghuang polysaccharide" is not a single molecule but a structurally heterogeneous family of β-glucans, heterogalactans, mannans and polysaccharide-protein complexes whose immune effects may be governed by the coupling of molecular structure × pattern-recognition receptor × cell type × host microenvironment. This review synthesizes current evidence across five layers - chemical structure, immune recognition, innate and adaptive cellular immunomodulation, immunometabolic regulation and the potential for trained immunity, and the gut microbiota-immune axis - and maps them onto immune-mechanism-based applications spanning tumor immune-microenvironment remodeling, barrier immunity and microbiota-associated regulation, host defense and inflammatory resolution, and immunometabolic disorders. We critically grade the receptor evidence, showing that most Sanghuang studies remain correlative (pathway phosphorylation or cytokine readouts) rather than demonstrating direct receptor engagement, in contrast to the benchmark fungal β-glucans lentinan, schizophyllan and PSK/Krestin, for which Dectin-1, Toll-like receptor and complement receptor 3 mechanisms are established. We further examine oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic constraints that shape whether luminal, gut-associated lymphoid or systemic mechanisms dominate. We propose a minimum reporting standard (Box 1) covering species authentication, extraction and purity control (including endotoxin and protein/phenolic contamination), structural characterization and receptor validation, and outline a multi-omics- and AI-enabled roadmap to move the field from asking "is it effective?" to "which structure, via which receptor, in which cell and which disease context?". Sanghuang polysaccharides therefore emerge as context-dependent immunomodulators rather than universal immune stimulants, and they represent a tractable model system for structure-defined fungal immunomodulators - but translation requires rigorous standardization and mechanistic validation.

articles.titulo: A nationally representative One Health multi-pathogen serosurvey in Cambodia: study protocol for the RACSMEI mixed-methods study.
articles.autores: Antoniolli A, Karlsson E, … Flamand C (41 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Cambodia faces a high and complex burden of zoonotic, vector-borne, vaccine-preventable and environmentally transmitted infections, driven by intensive human-animal-environment interactions. However, nationally representative data integrating human, animal and environmental dimensions of pathogen exposure remain limited. The RACSMEI (Risk Assessment of Community Spread of Multiple Endemic Infectious Diseases in a One Health Perspective) study aims to address this gap through a nationwide One Health serosurvey designed to generate policy-relevant epidemiological evidence for precision public health and integrated surveillance.
RACSMEI is a nationwide, cross-sectional, mixed-methods study conducted across all 25 provinces of Cambodia. Using a stratified, multi-stage cluster sampling design, approximately 15,000 individuals aged 2-75 years will be enrolled from 4,160 households in 104 randomly selected villages. Human, animal (poultry, pigs, dogs, cattle, small ruminants, rodents) and environmental (water, soil, air, surface swabs) samples will be collected. Exposure to more than 50 endemic, emerging, vaccine-preventable and elimination-targeted pathogens will be assessed using multiplex serological assays, molecular diagnostics and metagenomics sequencing approaches. Quantitative surveys will be complemented by semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions to explore social, behavioural and health system determinants of infection risk and care-seeking behaviours. Analyses will account for the complex survey design and integrate epidemiological, environmental and social science data.
By combining nationally representative sampling with integrated human, animal, environmental and social science data, RACSMEI aims to generate comprehensive evidence on infectious disease exposure and transmission risks across diverse socio-ecological contexts in Cambodia. The study will provide policy-relevant insights to support One Health surveillance strategies and targeted public health interventions. The protocol was approved by the Cambodian National Ethics Committee for Health Research and the Institutional Review Board of Institut Pasteur Paris.
The study is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07358910). It was retrospectively registered on 14 January 2026.

articles.titulo: Applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases: A systematic review.
articles.autores: Ong SQ, Brkljač B, … Hackenberger BK (8 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Mosquito-borne diseases (MBDs) remain a major global health challenge. Vector surveillance, pathogen detection, and clinical diagnosis are central to control efforts but are limited by labor-intensive workflows and shortages of trained personnel. Computer vision (CV) offers opportunities for scalable automation throughout the MBD management pipeline. We aimed to systematically characterize the applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases research, summarize methodological developments, and identify opportunities and barriers to translating these advances into public health practice. We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore for studies published between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2025, that applied computer vision to any aspect of MBD research or control. A total of 1,521 records were screened, and 650 studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies were categorized by computer vision application area, data types, algorithmic approaches, and data acquisition methods. Descriptive quantitative analysis and qualitative thematic synthesis were performed. The use of computer vision in MBD research increased significantly over the review period. Most studies focused on diagnostic applications, particularly Plasmodium detection in malaria microscopy. More recent work incorporated deep learning models for mosquito species classification, UAV- and satellite-based habitat mapping, and smartphone-based non-invasive diagnostic imaging. Emerging areas included 3D mosquito behavioral analysis and Internet of Things-enabled surveillance. Algorithmic approaches evolved from traditional image processing to convolutional neural networks, You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based object detectors, and transformer architectures. However, most models were developed using small, geographically-limited datasets, lacked external or prospective validation, and were rarely evaluated in operational settings, limiting their translational readiness.

articles.titulo: Intestinal Xdh overexpression promotes organismal aging with early redox dysregulation.
articles.autores: Pan S, Zhang F, … Li Y (11 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Oxidative stress accompanies aging, but whether a defined endogenous oxidant source can initiate tissue-to-organism aging remains unclear. We investigated xanthine oxidase (XO), an enzyme coupling purine catabolism to superoxide and hydrogen peroxide generation, using a human cross-sectional cohort and Drosophila genetic models. Among 442 adults, higher serum XO activity was independently associated with shorter relative leukocyte telomere length. Ubiquitous overexpression of xdh, the Drosophila xanthine oxidoreductase gene, shortened lifespan, accelerated locomotor decline, disrupted metabolic homeostasis, reduced antioxidant enzyme activities, and remodeled redox-, immune-, and metabolism-related transcriptional programs. Intestine-specific xdh overexpression was sufficient to reproduce organismal lifespan shortening and functional decline in both sexes. Intestinal xdh elevation increased intestinal DCF fluorescence and reduced total superoxide dismutase activity before detectable barrier leakage or expansion of culturable intestinal bacteria. These early redox abnormalities were followed by progressive barrier failure, increased bacterial burden, and reduced survival during hydrogen peroxide challenge. Intestinal transcriptomics further revealed early and persistent enrichment of oxidoreductase, glutathione, immune, and lipid-metabolic programs, with shared functional signatures across intestinal xdh overexpression, systemic xdh overexpression, and chronological aging. Collectively, these findings identify intestinal XO as a defined metabolic source of redox disruption capable of producing effects beyond the gut. They support a model in which sustained intestinal oxidative stress precedes and amplifies the loss of gut homeostasis, linking local redox disturbance to organismal aging phenotypes.

articles.titulo: HligTPS-mediated trehalose homeostasis links metabolic reprogramming to cold adaptation in Hylurgus ligniperda.
articles.autores: Cheng L, Han Y, … Tao J (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Overwintering adaptation is a critical determinant of whether invasive forest insects can overcome climatic constraints and successfully establish in newly invaded regions. Trehalose, a major cryoprotectant, is widely recognized as playing an essential role in cold adaptation. However, the dynamic regulatory mechanisms governing trehalose metabolism and its functional relationship with cold tolerance remain poorly understood. Here, naturally overwintering populations of Hylurgus ligniperda were used to investigate the role of trehalose-6-phosphate synthase (TPS)-mediated trehalose metabolism in cold adaptation through metabolomic analysis, RNA interference, and exogenous compensation experiments. Metabolomic profiling revealed extensive metabolic reprogramming during overwintering, with carbohydrate metabolism as the most significant enriched pathway. Trehalose accumulation closely paralleled seasonal changes in cold tolerance and peaked during mid-overwintering. The trehalose biosynthetic gene HligTPS was significantly induced during overwintering and under acute cold stress. Silencing HligTPS reduced trehalose content and elevated LT50 (from -8.3 ± 1.1 °C to -6.7 ± 1.0 °C), indicating impaired cold tolerance, whereas exogenous trehalose supplementation partially rescued this phenotype. Notably, moderate trehalose elevation enhanced cold tolerance, whereas excessive accumulation increased mortality. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that carbohydrate metabolic reprogramming contributes to overwintering adaptation and HligTPS-mediated trehalose biosynthesis as a key mechanism underlying cold adaptation in H. ligniperda. More importantly, our results suggest that cold tolerance depends on the maintenance of trehalose homeostasis rather than on trehalose accumulation alone. This study provides new insights into the metabolic basis of insect overwintering adaptation and the climatic adaptability of invasive forest pests.

articles.titulo: Tissue repair and regeneration: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic interventions.
articles.autores: Zhang M, He J, Li Q (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Tissue injury is a pervasive feature of human disease, yet adult mammals exhibit limited regenerative capacity. A central determinant of regenerative outcomes is the inflammatory response, which orchestrates tissue repair through mechanisms that are evolutionarily conserved from Drosophila to mammals. Following injury, inflammation drives debris clearance, promotes the release of cytokines and growth factors, and contributes to the restoration of functional cells. However, dysregulated or unresolved inflammation can impair healing, drive scar formation, and ultimately result in organ dysfunction or failure. Here, we focus on recent advances in the spatiotemporal regulation of inflammation during tissue repair that have reshaped our understanding of its underlying mechanisms. We synthesize findings on the dynamic progression of repair from inflammatory initiation to active resolution and stem cell activation, highlighting features of immune cell plasticity and heterogeneity within injury-specific microenvironments, as well as the existence of pivotal macrophage-fibroblast interactions. Furthermore, we delineate the pleiotropic and context-dependent roles of key cytokines and signaling pathways in coordinating these processes. Finally, we discuss current and emerging therapeutic strategies, emphasizing the paradigm shift from broad immunosuppression toward precise modulation of inflammatory networks to promote regeneration and prevent fibrosis. Future progress hinges on integrating multiomic spatial atlases, precision immunomodulation, and standardized therapeutic protocols to decipher and manipulate immune-regenerative crosstalk, thereby driving the development of next-generation regenerative therapies.
